Teething or something else? What to notice.

More drool and chewing can accompany a new tooth. Fever or a baby who seems unwell needs a closer look. Here is a way to separate useful observations from guesses.

By BabyBaby · November 12, 2026 · 5 min read

In this guide

Common signsFever and other symptomsWhen to get helpComfort for sore gumsA useful note for a clinicianSources

When your baby is unsettled and chewing everything, it is tempting to put the whole day down to teething. A more useful starting point is to describe what changed: sore gums, extra drool, a measured temperature, feeding, or how alert your baby seems.

You do not need to identify the cause on your own. If your baby seems unwell or something worries you, ask a clinician rather than waiting for a tooth to appear.

Get emergency help now if your baby has difficulty breathing, is hard to wake, has blue or grey lips, or has a first seizure. Use your local emergency service. See the NHS emergency warning signs.

What commonly goes with a new tooth?

The NHS lists sore, red gums where a tooth is emerging, more drooling, and more chewing among common teething signs. Some teeth come through with little or no discomfort. Timing varies: many babies begin around six months, but some start earlier or later.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) also describes mild gum discomfort, drooling, and chewing. These observations can help you describe the day, but they do not establish why your baby is upset. You can tell a clinician about gum changes and other symptoms together without deciding that one explains the other.

Do not explain away fever or diarrhea.

The AAP says teething does not cause fever, diarrhea, or excessive crying. The NHS likewise says there is no evidence that teething causes diarrhea. A tooth coming through is not a reason to dismiss those symptoms.

The NHS defines fever as 38°C (100.4°F) or higher. Use a digital thermometer according to its instructions and local healthcare guidance. Note the reading and method.

When should you ask for medical advice?

NHS fever guidance calls for urgent advice if a baby:

  • Is under three months and has a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher, or you think they have a fever.
  • Is three to six months and has a temperature of 39°C (102.2°F) or higher, or you think they have a fever.
  • Has signs of dehydration, such as nappies that are less wet than usual, or is not their usual self and you are worried.

Contact your clinician or local urgent medical advice service; seek help sooner whenever your baby seems unwell. For fever, diarrhea, or much more crying than usual, the AAP advises contacting your child's doctor.

This is not a complete list of reasons to seek care. Your question can be as simple as: “My baby is behaving differently, and I am not sure what to make of it.”

For sore gums, keep comfort simple.

When your baby is otherwise well, the NHS suggests a gentle gum rub with a clean finger, a suitable teething ring, or comforting play. Try one thing and see whether your baby wants it; there is no need to keep going if they turn away.

  • Cool a suitable teething ring in the fridge only as its instructions allow. The NHS says never to freeze it or tie it around a baby's neck.
  • Skip teething necklaces. The AAP warns that they can cause choking or strangulation.
  • Wipe drool gently. The NHS notes that gently wiping the face may help prevent a drool rash.

If your baby remains uncomfortable, ask a clinician or pharmacist about appropriate next steps. An unsettled day does not mean you have missed a special trick.

Write down the details you want to explain.

A short note can make a conversation easier when you are tired. You can use paper or wherever you normally record care. Useful details to have at hand include:

  • Your baby's age and when you first noticed the change.
  • Any temperature reading, the time, and the method used.
  • What changed about feeds, wet diapers, alertness, or crying compared with their usual day.
  • What you tried and what happened afterward.

Keep observations separate from your guess about the cause. “More chewing today” and “38°C at 4 p.m.” are clearer starting points than “bad teething.” A log cannot decide whether your baby is ill, and making one should never delay getting help.

You do not need a perfect record. Start with what concerns you most and let the clinician ask the next question.
